reply:
loop) also costs a pass's worth of work, so neither is clearly cheaper without measuring it. The current version also keeps only one collection, not two.

## `src/array/intersectionBy.ts`

**Building the lookup set (`intersectionBy.ts:40`)**: `secondArr.map(mapper)` makes a temporary array of size m just to fill the `Set`, so that's O(m) time plus an extra O(m) allocation. A `for` loop that adds straight to the `Set` would skip the temporary array. That only matters when m is large (around 10⁵ and up), and even then it's a constant-factor saving.
  - Unrelated to performance: because `.map` is used, `mapper` gets called as `(item, index, array)` for `secondArr` but with just `(item)` for `firstArr`. The type `(item: T | U) => unknown` hides the difference, but a mapper that accepts optional extra parameters would behave differently for the two arrays.

**Main loop (`:42-50`)**: one pass over `firstArr` (size n), with one `mapper` call, one `Set.has`, and on a match one `Set.delete`. That's O(n + m) overall. Deleting matched keys is cheap and also removes duplicates from the result. There's no `includes` or `indexOf` scan inside the loop that could make it O(n·m).

## Bottom line

Both functions already use the hash-based linear approach. The only real candidate is removing the temporary array in `intersectionBy`, and that's a small constant-factor saving. Under the repo's contribution rules it would need benchmark results showing a measurable gain before it's worth changing.

reply:
array length n and second array length m. Each element costs one `mapper` call and one `Set.has`.
- **Small constant-factor costs:**
  - Line 40, `new Set(secondArr.map(mapper))`, builds a temporary array of length m before building the `Set`. Adding each mapped value to the `Set` in a plain loop avoids that.
  - Lines 46–48 do `has` and then `delete`, which hashes the same key twice. `if (mappedSecondSet.delete(mappedItem)) result.push(item)` does it with one lookup, because `delete` returns whether the key was there.
- **Measured** (n = m = 100k): 8.29 ms now vs 7.98 ms with both changes, about 4%. That's within run-to-run variation.

### Something I noticed that isn't about speed
On line 40, `secondArr.map(mapper)` calls `mapper(item, index, array)`. The declared signature is `mapper(item)`, and line 44 calls it with one argument. A mapper that reads a second parameter would therefore behave differently on the two arrays. `parseInt` is the classic example, since it would treat the index as its radix.

### Recommendation
Neither function has a real performance problem. The changes above would save roughly 5–10%, and these numbers come from a quick one-off Node script, not the repo's `benchmarks/performance/*.bench.ts`. The project doesn't accept changes that only refactor, and performance work has to come with benchmark results. So these are only worth a PR if `yarn bench` shows a gain clearly above noise compared with lodash. Without that, I'd leave both files as they are.

It's the same O(n), just a slightly bigger constant per item. Changing it wouldn't count as a speed fix unless a benchmark shows a gain, so I'm not reporting it as a problem.
- **`Array.from(map.values())` (line 41):** one pass over the unique items, at most n. That's linear.

### `src/array/intersectionBy.ts`
- **Building the Set (line 40):** `secondArr.map(mapper)` maps all m items, then `new Set(...)` reads them all a second time. That's two linear passes plus a temporary array of m items. It's not quadratic. When m is large it costs one extra array of that size, but the asymptotic cost doesn't change.
- **Loop at line 42:** goes over `firstArr` once (n items), with `Set.has` and `Set.delete` costing about the same no matter how big the Set is. There's no `includes`/`indexOf` scan inside the loop, so a large n doesn't cause quadratic growth. Removing matched keys also keeps duplicates out of the output without needing a second lookup structure.

### An off-lens observation (correctness, not performance)
At line 40, `secondArr.map(mapper)` calls `mapper(item, index, array)`. The first array's loop at line 44 calls only `mapper(item)`. If a mapper uses a second parameter, the two arrays get mapped differently. With `parseInt`, for example, `['10','10']` maps to `[10, NaN]` in the second array, but to `10` for every item in the first. TypeScript accepts this because the declared signature has a single parameter. It's outside the Perf lens, but it may be worth a separate look.

reply:
rst. There are no nested scans.
- **Line 40, `new Set(secondArr.map(mapper))`:** this builds a throwaway array of m mapped values before filling the set. A plain `for` loop that adds `mapper(secondArr[i])` straight into the `Set` skips that array.
- **Lines 46–48, `has` then `delete`:** that's two hash lookups on every hit. `Set.prototype.delete` returns a boolean, so `if (mappedSecondSet.delete(mappedItem)) result.push(item);` needs only one.
- **Measured gain:** with both changes, the 10k × 10k case (5,000 matches, same as `benchmarks/performance/intersectionBy.bench.ts`) went from about 720–733 µs to 619–630 µs, roughly 14% faster.

**This change also fixes an inconsistency.** Because of `.map`, `mapper` is called as `(item, index, array)` for the second array but as `(item)` for the first. A mapper that reads the second argument gives different keys for the two sides. For example, with `parseInt` the index becomes the radix: `parseInt('10', 1)` is `NaN`, so the match is silently lost. The direct loop calls `mapper(item)` on both sides, which matches the declared `(item: T | U) => unknown` signature.
